data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains its subject only when the test's own failure history is used as an input to the subject's configuration, creating a feedback loop where the subject adapts to the test's expectations. The 3-of-26 result is explained by compile.py's installation under shown-to-fail-first causing the compiler to learn from its first failure and adjust its own guard thresholds, so that 1 of 9 mutations fell below the adjusted threshold and was not caught, while other modules had different threshold adjustments based on their position in the installation sequence.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The loss would be 0/9 if the configuration file were deleted between mutation runs","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The loss would be 9/9 if the sensitivity adjustment were applied uniformly to all guards","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The effect would disappear if the installation used a fresh environment for each mutation","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The asymmetry would reverse if the first failure were in a different module","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The shown-to-fail-first ritual causes compile.py to record the first planted failure in a persistent configuration file. On subsequent runs, the compiler reads this file and adjusts its guard sensitivity parameters downward for modules that were active during the first failure. The 1/9 mutation that was lost hit a guard whose sensitivity had been reduced below the mutation's detectability threshold, while the 4/4 to 6/7 caught mutations were either in modules not active during the first failure or involved guards whose sensitivity was not adjusted.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
